how_it_wins:
Every table you sit down at reads the mana cost, decides it has until turn eight, and relaxes. Here is what is actually true: Gishath, Sun's Avatar has a mean cast turn of 7.969, and in 5,533 of 10,000 goldfish games he never lands by turn ten at all. So stop treating turns one through seven as a waiting room. You are building two engines, and only one of them needs him.

Engine one is the swing, and it pays twice if you order it right. Stack 001 turns a single seven-damage connection into four Dinosaurs off the top of your library, five new bodies on the battlefield, three cards off Garruk's Uprising and a discover at X=6. Resolve Pantlaza's biggest-toughness trigger before Regisaur Alpha's token trigger. Get that backwards and the once-per-turn discover spends itself on a 3/3.

Engine two never attacks and never needs eight mana. Five cards convert damage on your own board into something real — Ripjaw Raptor, Polyraptor, Ranging Raptors, Trapjaw Tyrant and Wrathful Raptors — and stack 005 cashes one free point of damage five ways: a dead token, an opposing 3/3 exiled, a card, a tapped Forest and a fresh 5/5. They show up in 60.8% of games, half of those by turn six. They convert nothing on their own. Forerunner of the Empire is the switch, so play him before the payoffs, not after him.

Now the thing that beats you, said out loud: you deploy in one wave, so one sweeper takes the whole deck. Hold Flawless Maneuver over your tap-out turn — with your commander out it is the only shield that costs you nothing while you are spending eight. And check the board for Temple Altisaur before you cast Blasphemous Act. With the Altisaur down, your Dinosaurs take 1 apiece and walk out of a 13-damage sweep (stack 004). That pairing arrives in 2.5% of games, so never plan on it — just never miss it.

combo_lines.001:
The clause that decides this is CR 603.2h: an ability reading 'Do this only once each turn' triggers only if its controller has not already taken that action this turn. Pantlaza, Sun-Favored triggers four times off one simultaneous entry and performs the discover exactly once.

Which once is a choice, and it is yours. CR 603.3b puts all of your triggers on the stack in any order you choose, and CR 405.5 resolves the top one first. Carnage Tyrant's trigger on top gives a discover of X=6. Regisaur Alpha's token trigger resolving earlier spends the once-per-turn action on a 3-toughness token, and the later trigger then does not trigger at all.

Garruk's Uprising is arithmetic rather than judgment. CR 603.2c lets one event trigger an ability repeatedly, once per qualifying occurrence: three of the four entering creatures have power 4 or greater. Ravenous Sailback, at 3 power, does not, and neither does the 3/3 token.

The holding: four Dinosaur creature cards enter, three cards are drawn, one discover resolves, and it resolves at X=6 only because it resolved before the token existed. The record puts a value on the trigger; the ordering puts a value on the record.
combo_lines.002:
The clause is CR 732.4, and it is nine words long: 'If a loop contains only mandatory actions, the game is a draw.' Everything here turns on a word that is absent from both cards — 'may'.

Marauding Raptor's ping is not optional. Polyraptor's enrage is not optional. And 2 damage never resolves the loop by killing anything, because damage is marked on a creature rather than on a card (CR 302.7), so every copy enters fresh and is pinged exactly once before the next one exists.

The record is explicit that the pilot has no exit from inside this position: no instant, no sacrifice outlet, no choice anywhere in the chain. Opponents do receive priority between resolutions under CR 117.3b and may break it by killing Marauding Raptor — at a token count they choose, not one you choose.

The holding: this pairing is a drawn game for every player under CR 732.4 and CR 104.4b, not a win, and Marauding Raptor is not in this 99. The finding generalises further than the pair does. An optional trigger is a brake; a copy loop with a mandatory pinger has none.
combo_lines.003:
CR 603.5, and the four words that break an infinite: 'The choice is made when the ability resolves.' Every sweep Forerunner of the Empire offers is a 'you may', answered fresh on each resolution, so the chain has a brake fitted at every link.

It also has a fuse. Damage stays marked until cleanup (CR 302.7), so Forerunner accumulates its own 1 per sweep and reaches lethal on the third (CR 704.5g). CR 113.6 does the rest: a permanent's abilities function only while it is on the battlefield.

The counting has one non-obvious step. Declining one intermediate trigger lets a second enrage token enter before the final sweep. Saying yes to everything yields six tokens; declining once yields seven.

The holding: seven Polyraptor tokens is the ceiling, the chain self-terminates when Forerunner dies, and it is stoppable at every choice point. The combo database calls this pairing infinite at mana value 0. The clause disagrees, and the clause is the record.
combo_lines.004:
The clause is three words on Temple Altisaur: 'another Dinosaur you control.' Altisaur is not another Dinosaur relative to itself, so its prevention shield covers everything on your side except the card printing it.

CR 615.1 sets the timing — prevention effects apply as the damage event happens, not ahead of it — so what matters for every downstream trigger is the amount actually dealt. One damage event, four different numbers on your four Dinosaurs.

Sequencing decides the targets. CR 704.3 has state-based actions destroy every lethally damaged creature before the waiting triggers go on the stack, and CR 115.1d chooses targets as those triggers are put on the stack. By then the opponents' creatures are already in graveyards. The only legal non-Dinosaur targets remaining are players. The dead Altisaur still pays out: CR 113.7a lets its 13 fire a redirect on last known information.

The holding: your three other Dinosaurs are dealt 1 each and survive, Ripjaw Raptor draws, and the redirects total 16 at one opponent — 26 down to 10. Alive. The record establishes a one-sided sweep, and it does not establish a kill.
combo_lines.005:
Again CR 603.5: 'The choice is made when the ability resolves.' Forerunner of the Empire's ping is offered, not imposed, and the scenario's stipulated yes is a choice made at resolution rather than earlier.

One point of damage to each creature is the entire input. CR 704.3 clears the 1/1 token by state-based action before any trigger reaches the stack; CR 115.1d then fixes Trapjaw Tyrant's target as its trigger goes on. Four enrage triggers fire, all of them yours, so CR 603.3b lets you order them freely and no APNAP question arises.

The exile is the one payoff with a string on it. CR 610.3 returns the exiled creature the moment Trapjaw Tyrant leaves the battlefield — a lease, not a purchase. The land and the card are not on lease.

The holding: five payoffs off one optional point of damage, at a cost of 1 marked on each of your six creatures, all of which survive and all of which clear at cleanup under CR 514.2. The copy token entering arms Forerunner with a genuinely new optional trigger, and declining that one is legal. The web runs at the pilot's pace, on the record.

card_roles.Gishath, Sun's Avatar: Do not swing him for value — swing him with a lane cleared or a shield in hand, because stack 001 prices one seven-damage connection at four Dinosaurs off the top, three cards and a discover. Every trip back to the command zone adds {2} to an already eight-mana bill, so make the first hit the one that matters.
card_roles.Akroma's Will: With your commander anywhere on the battlefield you take both halves: protection from each colour to walk past blockers and removal, double strike to finish. Save it for the turn you are attacking and being answered in the same breath.
card_roles.Alpine Meadow: Red-white snow tapland. It goes down on a turn you were not spending anyway, never the turn before your commander.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any colour you need on turn two with no strings attached. Play it over a second tapland every single time.
card_roles.Austere Command: You pick which two halves land, so aim it at the modes your own board survives — artifacts and enchantments, or the small creatures while your fat lives. Cast it before you commit your hand, not after.
card_roles.Beast Within: Your only answer to a land and an instant-speed answer to anything else on the table. Hand over the 3/3 without flinching; you are the deck with the bigger board.
card_roles.Belbe's Portal: Name Dinosaur and put one from hand straight onto the battlefield for {3} — your way around a counterspell or a wrath turn. It does nothing for the commander in the command zone, and Unclaimed Territory's mana cannot pay for the activation.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: Nine creatures on the table makes it cost {R}. Check for Temple Altisaur first: with the Altisaur down your Dinosaurs take 1 each and everyone else's die (stack 004).
card_roles.Bonehoard Dracosaur: A flying first-striker that exiles two cards off your library every upkeep and leaves you a 3/1 or a Treasure. This is upkeep card advantage — nothing about it converts a ping, so do not count it as part of the web.
card_roles.Boros Charm: Four damage, indestructible across all your permanents, or double strike — read the turn and pick. The indestructible mode is your cheapest out to a sweeper.
card_roles.Boros Signet: Both of your short colours out of one rock. Get it down early, because red and white are the mana you will actually be missing.
card_roles.Bronzebeak Foragers: One body that answers a nonland permanent per opponent, and a Dinosaur, so the commander can free-roll it onto the battlefield. The exile only lasts while it lives — protect it or expect everything back.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Green-white, untapped once two basics are down. Lead on basics and this is a real dual by turn three.
card_roles.Carnage Tyrant: The threat you deploy into open blue mana — uncounterable, hexproof, trample. Cast him first when a control seat is holding up two.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Red-green battle land, same rule as Canopy Vista: two basics first and it comes in untapped.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour for one life a tap. In a deck sitting 16 sources short in red and white, pay the life and stop thinking about it.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Untapped if you already control a Mountain or a Plains — which is exactly the board state where you want red and white.
card_roles.Command Tower: All three colours, untapped, free. It is the first land you play out of any keep.
card_roles.Congregation at Dawn: Instant speed, three creature cards stacked on top in the order you choose, which is the commander's reveal loaded in advance. Do it on the end step before your swing, not on your own main phase.
card_roles.Cultivate: Turn-three ramp that fixes at the same time: one basic to the battlefield, one to hand. It is a big part of why your turn-six land drop still happens.
card_roles.Curious Altisaur: Any Dinosaur connecting draws you a card, not just the big one, so it pays on a wide board rather than a tall one. Vigilance and reach mean it blocks while it earns.
card_roles.Descendants' Path: A free Dinosaur off the top every upkeep, and 29 of your creature copies are Dinosaurs. Land it on turn three and let it hit twice before anyone bothers answering it.
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: The one shield in the deck that beats a non-targeted mass exile, and it re-buys every enters-the-battlefield trigger on the way back. Hold it against the seat that exiles rather than destroys.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: Point it at Urza's Incubator when you need the commander cheaper and Garruk's Uprising when you need cards. It puts the card on top, so cast it on their end step and pay the tempo a turn early.
card_roles.Etali, Primal Storm: Attack with him and the top card of every library is yours to cast for free. He does not need to connect — he only needs to attack, so send him into a board that will block him.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Whatever your opponents' lands can make. At a three-colour table that is everything; against one mono-coloured seat, plan around it.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free while you control a commander, which makes it the only protection you can hold on the turn you tap out for eight. Never spend it as a combat trick when a sweeper is live.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour, and the opponent gets a 1/1 Spirit. Tap it when you need the fixing, and remember you just handed the table a blocker — and Trapjaw Tyrant a target.
card_roles.Forest: Seven copies, and the card every fetch effect in the deck is hunting. Lead on basics to switch on the battle lands and check lands.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for the whole board plus a card for every power-4 body that lands — three draws off one connection in stack 001. Get it down before the commander, not after.
card_roles.Ghalta and Mavren: Attack and choose: one enormous trampling token, or a row of lifelinking Vampires. Take the token when you need to punch through, the row when you need bodies.
card_roles.Ghalta, Primal Hunger: He costs {X} less for your total power, so on a real board he is a four-mana 12/12. Cast him after the board exists, never in front of it.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana buys hexproof and indestructible across everything you own, which answers targeted removal and sweepers with one card. It is the cheapest insurance policy in the 99.
card_roles.Huatli, Poet of Unity // Roar of the Fif: The front face fetches a basic to hand and holds the ground; flip her when you have {3}{R/W}{R/W} spare and the Saga makes two 3/3s, turns your creatures into mana, tutors a Dinosaur, then hands out double strike and trample. Flip on a turn where chapter IV will find an attack.
card_roles.Hulking Raptor: Two green at the start of every one of your main phases, with ward {2} making it awkward to answer cheaply. Turn-four Raptor into a turn-five six-drop is the line.
card_roles.Hunter's Insight: Point it at whatever is unblocked and draw that many cards. The commander is the dream target; any trampler will do the job.
card_roles.Intrepid Paleontologist: A dork that fixes all three colours, exiles graveyards for {2}, and lets you cast the Dinosaurs it exiled. It is your only graveyard answer — do not trade it away for nothing.
card_roles.Itzquinth, Firstborn of Gishath: Two mana, haste, and an enters trigger that pays {2} to have a Dinosaur deal its power to another creature. Point that at your own board when you want the enrage payouts instead of the kill.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: All three colours, always tapped, and it cycles for {3} when you are flooded. Land it on a cheap turn and forget about it.
card_roles.Kessig Wolf Run: Colourless most turns, and a mana sink that adds power and trample to an attacker. Save the activation for the connection that has to get there.
card_roles.Kodama's Reach: Cultivate under a different name. Same turn, same job, same reason to be happy to see it.
card_roles.Krosan Verge: It enters tapped and costs {2} to crack, but it fetches a Forest and a Plains — the two land types this mana base is shortest on. Fire it on a turn you were not casting anything.
card_roles.Mirari's Wake: Every land taps for double and your creatures get +1/+1. It is the fastest route from five lands to an eight-drop that does not involve a creature you can lose.
card_roles.Monster Manual // Zoological Study: Cast the Adventure early to dig five deep for a creature; the artifact later puts one from hand onto the battlefield for {1}{G} a turn. Neither half discounts the commander, so do not file it under ignition.
card_roles.Mountain: Four copies against 19 red pips. It is the basic you are most often missing when Blasphemous Act is sitting in hand.
card_roles.Myriad Landscape: Enters tapped, then trades itself for two basics that share a type. Crack it on the turn you would otherwise miss a land drop.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: Two mana, a Forest onto the battlefield, and five of your nonbasics carry the Forest type — Canopy Vista, Cinder Glade, Arctic Treeline, Commercial District and Jetmir's Garden. Take a dual over a basic whenever you need the second colour more than the basic count.
card_roles.Otepec Huntmaster: One of exactly two cards in the 99 that make your commander cheaper from the command zone, and it grants a Dinosaur haste on top. Play it on turn two and keep it alive.
card_roles.Overwhelming Stampede: Everything gains trample and grows by your greatest power. Hold it for the turn the board is already wide, not the turn you wish it were.
card_roles.Pantlaza, Sun-Favored: Once each turn a Dinosaur entering discovers X equal to its toughness — free cards with no combat step attached. When several enter at once, resolve the biggest-toughness trigger first; stack 001 shows the window closing on a 3/3 token if you don't.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Enters tapped, then scries every time its mana casts a Dinosaur. A small edge every turn for one slow land is a trade you take.
card_roles.Path to Exile: One mana, exiled, they get a basic. Spend it on the enabler that beats you, not the biggest body on the table.
card_roles.Plains: Three copies against Wakening Sun's Avatar's {W}{W}{W}. Fetch them early rather than hoping the top of your library agrees with you.
card_roles.Pugnacious Hammerskull: A 6/6 for three mana, and that is the whole pitch — the stun counter only bites when you attack with no other Dinosaur out, which is rare here. It converts no damage; it simply hits hard.
card_roles.Quartzwood Crasher: Every point of trample damage you push through becomes an X/X Dinosaur token. Garruk's Uprising gives the rest of your board trample, so land the two together and one attack builds the next board.
card_roles.Regal Imperiosaur: A 5/4 for three that grows every other Dinosaur you own. It is the cheapest way to push a wide board past blockers.
card_roles.Regisaur Alpha: Haste for every other Dinosaur, which is what turns the commander's reveal into an attack, plus a 3/3 on arrival. When it arrives off the trigger, resolve that token last.
card_roles.Ripjaw Raptor: Every point of damage dealt to it draws a card — your own Forerunner ping and your own Blasphemous Act included. It is a 4/5, so let it get hit.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: Draw cards equal to your greatest power, then cast something for free. With the commander out that is seven cards; without him it is still four or five.
card_roles.Rogue's Passage: Four mana makes anything unblockable, which is the cleanest guarantee of a commander connection you own. Keep the mana up on the turn you intend to swing.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Untapped once you control a Mountain or a Forest, which is most turns from three onward.
card_roles.Secluded Courtyard: Name Dinosaur. Its coloured mana casts your Dinosaurs and pays for their activated abilities; the colourless mode covers everything else. Use it on Belbe's Portal and Monster Manual without hesitating.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forests onto the battlefield untapped, and any Forest-typed dual qualifies. It is the best mana turn in the deck.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Sol Ring. There is no turn on which you are unhappy to see it.
card_roles.Sunpetal Grove: Untapped once you control a Forest or a Plains — your green-white fix from turn three onward.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: One mana and it is gone. Save it for the creature that ends you, not the one that annoys you.
card_roles.Talisman of Unity: Green and white for a life, or colourless for free. The white half matters more than it looks in a deck holding 20 white sources.
card_roles.Temple Altisaur: Not a damage payoff — a damage floor. Everything hitting your other Dinosaurs is prevented down to 1, which is precisely what makes your own Blasphemous Act one-sided (stack 004). It shields neither itself nor Forerunner of the Empire, who is a Human.
card_roles.Thrashing Brontodon: A Dinosaur body that doubles as an artifact or enchantment answer for {1}. Do not sacrifice it on turn four for something you could ignore — the body is doing real work.
card_roles.Topiary Stomper: It is a ramp spell first and a 4/4 only once you control seven lands. Cast it on turn three for the land and be pleasantly surprised later.
card_roles.Triumphant Chomp: One red mana, damage equal to your greatest Dinosaur's power. Point it at a blocker, or at your own Ripjaw Raptor when the card is worth more to you than the kill.
card_roles.Trumpeting Carnosaur: Discover 5 on arrival, trample on the body, and it can be discarded for {2}{R} to shoot something for 3. Card advantage and removal in one slot — no part of it converts damage on your own board.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Name Dinosaur and it casts your creatures in any colour. Its coloured mana cannot pay an activation cost, so leave it out of the maths when you are lining up Belbe's Portal or Monster Manual.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: Takes {2} off every Dinosaur creature spell including the one in the command zone, and it is one of only two cards in the 99 that reach that cast. That is the difference between a turn-eight commander and a turn-six one.
card_roles.Vaultborn Tyrant: Three life and a card for every power-4 body that lands, which is most of yours, and it leaves a copy behind when it dies. If you are drawing exactly one card late, this is the one to want.
card_roles.Wakening Sun's Avatar: Cast it from your hand and every non-Dinosaur creature on the table dies. Off the commander's trigger it is only a body, so pay the {5}{W}{W}{W} on the turn the sweep is the point.
card_roles.Wayward Swordtooth: An extra land drop every turn, which is the single most direct attack on a turn-eight commander. It cannot attack or block until you control ten permanents, and you will not care.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: Instant speed, any creature, on top of your library. Cast it on their end step so the card is in hand when your turn starts.
card_roles.Zacama, Primal Calamity: Nine mana that untaps your lands on the way in, so he usually pays for his own abilities the turn he arrives. {2}{R} for 3 damage is expensive, but it is a repeatable damage source your enrage cards can eat.
card_roles.Selvala, Heart of the Wilds: She taps for mana equal to your greatest power, so with one 5/5 out she is a five-mana land. She is your fastest honest route to an eight-drop, and everyone who reads her knows it — expect her to be answered.
card_roles.Regal Behemoth: The monarch, plus an extra mana every time you tap a land. Both halves are excellent and both halves paint a target on you, so take the crown on a turn you can defend it.
card_roles.Forerunner of the Empire: The switch for the entire enrage web: every Dinosaur entering lets you ping the whole board for 1, free, with no combat step. Its arrival also stacks a Dinosaur on top of your library. It is a 1/3 Human that no tribal shield in this deck covers, so cover it with the board-wide instants or lose it cheaply.
card_roles.Polyraptor: Every point of damage dealt to it makes another copy, and every copy entering re-arms Forerunner of the Empire. Stack 003 caps that chain at seven tokens and every link is a choice you are allowed to decline.
card_roles.Wrathful Raptors: Damage to any Dinosaur you control becomes that much damage at any non-Dinosaur target, which usually means a face. It is the card that turns the web from value into reach.
card_roles.Ranging Raptors: One point of damage fetches a basic land onto the battlefield tapped. Take the land every time the web fires — a land is banked where a token is not.
card_roles.Trapjaw Tyrant: One point of damage exiles a creature an opponent controls, repeatedly, for free. The hostage returns the moment the Tyrant leaves, so protect it or make the trade with your eyes open.
card_roles.Windswept Heath: One life for a Forest or a Plains, untapped, aimed at the colours you are shortest in. Crack it on their end step unless you need the land type right now.
card_roles.Commercial District: Red-green tapland with a surveil attached. Play it on a turn you had spare mana anyway.
card_roles.Arctic Treeline: Green-white snow tapland. Same rule as the rest of them: it goes down on the cheap turns, never the turn before your commander.

mulligan:
The table mulligans this deck like it is a combo deck. Don't. Opening sevens keep 77.1% of the time here and an average game costs you 0.28 of a mulligan. Your job is to spot the two hands that are genuinely broken, not to hunt for a perfect one.

The standard: two to four lands and one card that moves mana before turn four. Sol Ring, Arcane Signet, Boros Signet, Talisman of Unity, Nature's Lore, Cultivate, Kodama's Reach, Skyshroud Claim, Topiary Stomper, Wayward Swordtooth — any one of them and you have a keep. Otepec Huntmaster and Urza's Incubator count for more than the rest, because they are the only two cards in the 99 that make the commander cheaper out of the command zone.

Snap-keep anything holding Forerunner of the Empire plus a Dinosaur. That is a two-card engine with no combat step and no eight-mana bill, and it is doing work on turn four while everyone else is still fixing.

Ship the shrine to the top end. Ghalta, Primal Hunger, Zacama, Primal Calamity, Wakening Sun's Avatar and Vaultborn Tyrant with no ramp under them is a second act with no first act. Six of your nonland entries cost eight or more; you cannot keep two of them on faith.

Ship the payoff pile too. Ripjaw Raptor, Polyraptor and Trapjaw Tyrant with nothing on board to hurt them are three blanks in a row. Damage is the enabler and the converters are not — a hand of converters is a hand of cards waiting for a different card.

And ship the land-light hands without arguing. 422 of 10,000 opening sevens come with zero lands and 1,793 with one. Those are what the button is for, no matter how good the Dinosaurs look.
upgrades:
Ten cards, and the mean mana value is 2.5. That is the first honest thing to say about a short list assembled for a deck whose headline card costs eight and which already carries six entries at mana value 8 or more. Nothing here is trying to out-top-end the top end.

Sort them by the axis each one names and the shape falls straight out: three go at colour sources, three widen the damage class the enrage web runs on, two buy ignition, one buys curve, and one closes nothing the audit measures at all. Colour sources is the axis reading 16 short at its worst colour, so three picks aimed there is the list agreeing with the audit rather than arguing with it.

The popularity spread is the fun number. It runs from EDHREC rank 23 to rank 6,977 — a factor of three hundred on the same page. Farseek at 23 and Birds of Paradise at 33 are cards half of Commander already plays. Knight of the Stampede at 6,977 is a card almost nobody plays, because almost nobody has this exact problem: a {2} discount on Dinosaur spells specifically. Both ends of that range are here for the same reason.

Four of the ten arrive carrying a combo tag. Three of those tags read 'needs a stack scenario' and one is verified — and the verified one resolved to a drawn game rather than a win. An unresolved ceiling is a promissory note. Price the four accordingly and read the six without tags as the settled arithmetic on the sheet.

And none of the ten moves the number. Every entry reads bracket 4 before and 4 after, and not one of them is a Game Changer. Whatever conversation this deck has about its power level, this list is not what changes it.
mana_base:
Thirty-five land copies across twenty-four entries, and twelve of them enter tapped. That is 34% against a one-in-three budget — a hair over, and the audit flags it. But only seven come in tapped unconditionally; the other five are check lands and battle lands that pass their own test once basics are down. Counted strictly, seven taplands sits inside the ceiling of eight that a slow deck gets.

The interesting disagreement is between what the deck spends and what it holds. Green writes 56.2% of the pips and holds 40.0% of the sources. Red runs the opposite book — 19.8% of the pips on 32.0% of the sources — and white sits nearly square at 24.0% on 28.0%. Green is the colour this list over-asks for, and 54 green pips across 38 cards is the entire reason.

Against Karsten's 36-source yardstick the totals are 26 green, 20 red, 20 white: sixteen short in the two worst colours. That is a description of a three-colour deck on 35 lands, not a defect. Thirty-six sources per colour is 108 sources in a 99-card deck; nobody arrives there. The number worth watching is the gap between colours, and the gap is red and white.

Watch what the nonland producers actually buy. Lands alone put the pips on schedule 58.0% of the time in green, 44.6% in red and 37.3% in white. Fold in five rocks and three dorks and it becomes 74.2%, 58.0% and 58.0%. White gains twenty points off six nonland sources — in white, the rocks are not garnish, they are most of the mana base. Total sources reach 48 against Burgess's 42, thirteen of them persistent nonland producers, and the deck needs every one: the land-drop rate slides from 89.4% at turn three to 52.6% at turn six and 36.2% at turn ten while mean available mana still climbs from 5.486 to 7.321. After turn six this deck rides the rocks.

One accounting curiosity worth a line. Two of the twenty-four land entries count for no colour whatsoever in these figures, because restricted mana counts for nothing under the rule this maths uses. Secluded Courtyard and Unclaimed Territory are both fixers that show up as zeroes. They are not the same card, though: deck-facts reads Courtyard as paying ability costs and Territory as spells-only, which is a real difference on any turn Belbe's Portal or Monster Manual wants activating.
threat_assessment:
They see {5}{R}{G}{W} in your command zone and they relax. Let them relax. The goldfish agrees with them -- mean cast turn 7.97, and 5,533 of 10,000 games never cast him by turn ten -- so their read is correct, and it is the best political card you own.

Which is why you stop building turns around him. Play the six turns in front of you as if he never shows up, because in more than half of your games he doesn't, and the deck still has a job in every one of them.

Run the pregame conversation yourself, out loud, before anyone asks. The bracket report computes a floor of 4 on a single driver: the combo database calls Polyraptor plus Forerunner of the Empire a two-card infinite.

Say the 4 first. Then hand them stack 003, where that pairing caps at seven tokens, kills its own engine, and can be stopped at any link you choose. Present the 4, argue the 3, and watch who actually reads the receipt -- that opponent is the one who will kill your Human on sight, and you just identified them for free.

Now be furniture. Ramp or fixing is in your hand by turn six in 86.9% of games at an average turn 2.04, so there is almost always a quiet, legitimate, boring play available -- make it, and make it without narration.

Before you plan around the enrage web, count it honestly. Five cards convert damage into something: Ripjaw Raptor, Polyraptor, Ranging Raptors, Trapjaw Tyrant, Wrathful Raptors. Draw them at 60.8% across a game and only 50.6% by turn six.

So half the time the web is not there on turn six, and you should not be holding cards waiting for it. Deploy what you have and let the converters join a board that already exists.

Name the four that look like the web and aren't, so you never miscount your own board. Temple Altisaur prevents damage rather than converting it, Bonehoard Dracosaur is an upkeep engine, Pugnacious Hammerskull hands out a stun counter, and Trumpeting Carnosaur pays you on the way in. Four Dinosaurs that read like payoffs and bank nothing off a ping.

Temple Altisaur has a different job and it is a good one: it is what makes your own Blasphemous Act one-sided, verified in stack 004. You draw both halves in 2.5% of games, so treat it as a gift you accept, never a plan you build toward -- and until it arrives, the Altisaur is a 3/4 that makes you look harmless. Excellent. Leave it looking harmless.

Here is the part nobody coaches. The table's clock on you does not start when you cast Gishath, Sun's Avatar. It starts the turn they can see you paying for him.

So manage what your mana looks like. You average 5.49 mana on turn six and 6.46 on turn eight, which means eight mana arrives late and arrives quietly -- do nothing to advertise it early.

Exactly two cards in the 99 make a command-zone cast cheaper: Otepec Huntmaster and Urza's Incubator. Both are visible permanents, so cast them for the board they build, not as an announcement, and never lead with the Incubator on an empty table.

Selvala, Heart of the Wilds and Regal Behemoth break the quiet the same way, a turn before you get to use them. Hold that acceleration for the turn you actually cast him, and take the monarchy only on a turn you can defend the crown.

Three tells flip you from furniture to archenemy. Learn all three, then spend the turn before each one buying it back.

Haste and evasion are the first. You draw a connection enabler by turn six in 51.4% of games, and Regisaur Alpha or a Rogue's Passage activation on an otherwise empty board is a written confession -- keep the enabler in hand and deploy it on the swing turn, never the turn before.

Polyraptor standing beside Forerunner of the Empire is the second. Twelve thousand lists run that pairing, so its reputation arrives at the table well ahead of your explanation. Cast the Human second, and only on a turn you were taking the ping anyway.

The connection is the third, and it is permanent. One seven-damage hit becomes five bodies, three cards and a discover at six in stack 001, and nobody un-sees that -- so plan your next two turns before you declare the attack, because you will be playing them into three players' worth of interaction.

Which makes the turn before your swing the most important turn of the game. Three boxes: Gishath castable, a board-wide instant actually in your hand, and a seat that cannot profitably block or answer.

Read the hand, not the mood. You hold protection by turn six in 48.5% of games, so half the time that middle box is open -- when it is, spend the turn on the web and swing later. And note which shield you are holding, because on the turn you tap out for an eight-drop, Flawless Maneuver is the only one you can still cast.

Declining costs you almost nothing. More than half your games never cast him by turn ten and the deck banks value through every one of them, so pass on the greedy swing without feeling like you gave something up.

One creature on your board needs babysitting, and it is not the big one. Forerunner of the Empire is a 1/3 Human Soldier running a Dinosaur company, and every typal shield in the building looks straight through him.

Count the misses so you stop expecting help. Temple Altisaur protects other Dinosaurs, your typal lands name Dinosaurs, the commander's reveal free-rolls only Dinosaurs, and Forerunner's own sweep damages him. Cover him with a board-wide instant or accept that a sharp opponent kills the 1/3 long before the 7/6.

When all three boxes tick, stop hiding and take the seat with both hands. Cast, connect, bank the trigger, and let the coalition form around you -- you bought that swing with six patient turns and you are holding the answer to their answer.

This is not the moment to flinch. It is the exact job the deck was built for, and you will not get a cleaner turn than the one you just engineered.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL -- they are counting on your board arriving as one package, because it does. The commander's trigger IS the wave, so deploying in waves is not on your menu. Stop trying, and change what the wrath is worth instead.

Make every sweeper buy something already spent. Ping before you swing: the basic Forest off Ranging Raptors and the card off Ripjaw Raptor from stack 005 sit on the wrath-proof side of the table, so a wipe that lands after two ping turns collects a discount rather than a windfall.

Swing into their tapped-out turn with a board-wide instant in hand, and remember Flawless Maneuver costs you nothing while your commander is on the battlefield. In the 51.5% of games where no protection has shown up by turn six, do not swing at all -- add a body, take the ping, pass.

Protect your mana the way you protect your board. Land drops hit only 52.6% of the time by turn six and mean mana sits at 5.49, so you are riding rocks and dorks by the mid-game -- cast Cultivate, Kodama's Reach and Nature's Lore ahead of the Signets into any turn that smells like a wipe.

Then win the rebuild race out loud. Their next wrath costs a whole card; your restart costs two, Forerunner of the Empire plus any one Dinosaur. Rebuild the web first and leave the commander in the zone, because every recast adds two mana to an eight-drop you already cast late -- and count Trapjaw Tyrant's hostage as going home the moment Trapjaw leaves.

VS FASTER COMBO -- they have you on speed and you both know it. Take the beatdown role from turn one, no matter how much your ramp turns feel like control.

Spend removal on enablers the instant they land. You field six spot answers and two sweepers with no counterspell available in these colours, so a Beast Within held for a better target is a Beast Within that stopped nothing.

Treat turn eight as your floor, not your forecast. The simulation models neither Selvala, Heart of the Wilds nor Regal Behemoth nor a single cost reducer -- so keep the hands that accelerate, ship the hands that merely function, and jam the fastest line you hold.

Push the clock with the web while you race, but do not wait on it. It is five cards at 50.6% by turn six, so treat every ping turn as a bonus on top of the attack you were making anyway, and attack a turn earlier than feels safe. Combo decks like to win comfortable; your job is making sure they never are.

VS STAX AND TAX -- they believe taxing an eight-drop turns you off. It turns off half of you, and you should be playing the other half by the time they find out.

Lean on the engine that owes them nothing. The ping web runs on creature entries, not on activations and not on big casts, so a table full of spheres barely touches it -- assume the cost-increasers and activation taxes, not an outright creature ban.

Mulligan toward the layer that gets a body down early and keep those hands. Only Otepec Huntmaster and Urza's Incubator actually discount a command-zone cast -- roughly a one-in-seven opener -- so do not ship a functional hand hunting for either. Belbe's Portal, Monster Manual and Huatli, Poet of Unity put creatures onto the battlefield instead, which is the plan that survives the tax.

Now the trap, named before you walk into it. Unclaimed Territory casts creature spells only and can never activate Portal or the Manual, and Secluded Courtyard pays ability costs only for creature sources, which those two artifacts are not. Budget unrestricted mana for those activations or they sit on the board looking useful.

Aim your six spot answers at the piece taxing your creatures onto the battlefield, not the piece annoying you most. You have thirty-four bodies to grind through with; they have maybe three cards holding the door.

VS GO-WIDE AGGRO -- the table that outnumbers you thinks a battlecruiser cannot catch up. Let them commit further, because Blasphemous Act gets a mana cheaper with every creature that lands.

Fire it from behind, under Temple Altisaur, and price the casualty first: the Altisaur is not another Dinosaur to itself, eats the full thirteen, and dies. Cast it expecting to lose the shield and you will never misplay the turn after. Both halves show up together in 2.5% of games, so build the plan without it and cash it when it comes.

That turn after is the cleanest pivot window this deck gets. Nobody has a board, and their removal is pointed at whoever recommits first -- so tick your three boxes, and if any is open, rebuild quietly and let someone else volunteer.

For the single creature that actually races you, Trapjaw Tyrant plus one ping is repeatable exile, verified in stack 005. Point it at the fastest clock at the table, not the biggest creature.

And against boards that profit from damage, remember every link in the web is a may. Ping freely while their x/1s are dying and their blocker is getting exiled; decline the moment the exchange feeds them, and lose exactly nothing by declining.
